content.text:
Done. Here's the summary.

## The hang

In `BrowserTabsClient.Query` (the code path a save hits for any Chrome window, running **synchronously on the UI thread**), the timeout only bounded the *connection* wait:

```csharp
Task connect = server.WaitForConnectionAsync();
if (!connect.Wait(timeout)) { ... }          // bounded (3s)
NativeMessaging.WriteFrame(server, ...);
string? reply = NativeMessaging.ReadFrame(server);   // UNBOUNDED blocking read
```

Once the native host connected to the pipe but didn't reply (extension loaded but stuck, host crashing after connect, handshake stall), `ReadFrame` → `Stream.Read` blocked the UI thread **forever**. That's the freeze on save, and it only appeared after the Chrome feature because nothing else does pipe I/O during capture.

## The fix

- **`NativeMessaging.cs`** — added `WriteFrameAsync`/`ReadFrameAsync` (+ an async read-exactly helper) that honor a `CancellationToken`, using true async pipe I/O (the pipe is already `PipeOptions.Asynchronous`). The existing sync methods are untouched — the native host still uses them on its background relay threads.
- **`BrowserTabsClient.cs`** — `Query` now runs the whole exchange (connect → request → reply) under a single `CancellationTokenSource(timeout)`. If any stage stalls, the token fires and it throws `BrowserUnavailableException`, so the adapter reports Chrome as uncapturable instead of hanging. Total time is now bounded to the 3s timeout rather than 3s + unbounded.
- **`BrowserTabsClientTests.cs`** — regression test: a client that connects and goes silent, plus the no-host case, both asserting `Query` gives up within budget. Fails against the old code, passes now.

**README.md** — added a Chrome bullet to the intro feature list (it restores tabs now, like VS Code and Terminal); the detailed setup section was already added with the feature.

All 109 tests pass, no warnings.

## Commit message (yours to make)

```
fix: bound the Chrome tabs pipe exchange so save can't hang

Query only timed out the pipe connection; the reply read after it was an
unbounded blocking read on the UI thread, so a native host that connected
but never answered froze the app on save. Make the whole exchange async
under one cancellation deadline, add async native-messaging framing, and
cover it with a regression test. Note Chrome tab restore in the README intro.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

One thing worth a look when you test live: if your extension *is* installed and this was reproducing, the host is connecting but not replying — the fix stops the freeze, but you'll now see a capture failure for that Chrome window, which points at the host↔extension handshake in `extension/background.js` / `BrowserHost`. 1	# Spike: Chrome native messaging
2	
3	What it takes to read the open tabs of each Chrome window, and to reopen them, findings for Google
4	Chrome on this machine (Chrome 157, `C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe`)
5	
6	Chrome does not expose its open tabs to another process, only an extension can read `chrome.tabs`,
7	and an extension can only talk to a local program through native messaging, so the shape is:
8	
9	```
10	Sessions app  <--named pipe-->  native host (spawned by Chrome)  <--stdio frames-->  Chrome  <-->  our MV3 extension
11	```
12	
13	the native host is a thin relay, Chrome owns its lifetime, our app owns the pipe
14	
15	## Host registration (Windows)
16	
17	A native messaging host is registered per user with a registry key whose default value is the full
18	path to a manifest JSON file:
19	
20	- key, `HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts\<host.name>`
21	- default value, the absolute path to `manifest.json`
22	
23	Verified on this machine, the key path is correct (Chrome already has
24	`com.microsoft.browsercore` registered there), and we can create, read back, and delete our own
25	`HKCU\...\NativeMessagingHosts\com.sessions.browser` key, so no admin rights are needed, HKCU is enough
26	
27	Manifest shape:
28	
29	```json
30	{
31	  "name": "com.sessions.browser",
32	  "description": "Sessions browser relay",
33	  "path": "C:\\full\\path\\to\\BrowserHost.exe",
34	  "type": "stdio",
35	  "allowed_origins": [ "chrome-extension://<EXTENSION_ID>/" ]
36	}
37	```
38	
39	- `path` is the host executable, Chrome launches it as a child process of `chrome.exe`
40	- `type` is always `stdio`
41	- `allowed_origins` must list the exact extension id with the trailing slash, a wrong id means Chrome
42	  refuses to launch the host with "forbidden" and the extension sees a disconnect
43	
44	## The extension id gotcha (pin it)
45	
46	For an unpacked extension with no `key` in its manifest, Chrome derives the 32-character id from the
47	SHA-256 of the extension's absolute folder path (bytes mapped to the letters a-p), so the id CHANGES
48	if the folder moves, which would break `allowed_origins`,
49	
50	Fix, pin the id by putting a `key` (base64 of a DER public key) in the extension `manifest.json`, then
51	the id is derived from the key and is stable wherever the folder sits, the install step computes the
52	same id from that key and writes it into `allowed_origins`,
53	
54	id derivation, first 16 bytes of SHA-256(DER public key), each 4-bit nibble mapped 0-15 to a-p
55	
56	This is the single most error-prone part, confirm the id in `chrome://extensions` matches the one in
57	`allowed_origins` after install
58	
59	## Message framing
60	
61	Each message both ways is a 4-byte little-endian unsigned length, then that many bytes of UTF-8 JSON,
62	verified by round-trip, `{"cmd":"getWindows"}` frames as `14 00 00 00` then the 20 JSON bytes,
63	
64	Hard rules for the host:
65	- stdout carries ONLY framed messages, any stray `print`/log byte on stdout corrupts the stream and
66	  Chrome kills the host, all logging must go to stderr or a file

This is the real bug, and the design doc names it. Per the spike (lines 74–83): the app is meant to be a **named-pipe server "listening while it runs,"** so the host connects once and **holds** the connection — that long-lived port is also what keeps Chrome's MV3 service worker alive.

But the implementation made the server **on-demand**: `BrowserTabsClient.Query` opens the pipe for ~3s only during a Save, then disposes it. So in steady state there's no server, the host's `Connect` fails, the host exits ("Native host has exited"), the extension reconnects every 1s and flaps forever — and a Save only succeeds if a host launch happens to land inside that 3s window. That's why capture reports "No response from the Chrome extension."

content.text:
Done. Here's the full picture.

## What was wrong (two separate bugs)

1. **The hang on save** — `BrowserTabsClient.Query` bounded only the pipe *connection*; the reply read after it was an unbounded blocking read on the UI thread. A host that connected but didn't reply froze the app. **Fixed** (first turn): the whole exchange now runs under one cancellation deadline via async I/O.

2. **The handshake never worked** — the real reason Chrome capture failed. The spike doc intends the app to be a pipe server the host can rely on, but the code only opened the pipe for ~3s during a Save. So the **host exited** whenever the app wasn't mid-capture ("Native host has exited"), the extension reconnected every second ("Error communicating with the native messaging host" — the flapping in your console), and a Save only worked if a host launch happened to land in that 3s window.

## The fix (patient host — your pick)

Rewrote `src/Sessions.BrowserHost/Program.cs` only:
- `pipe.Connect()` now **waits indefinitely** for the app's pipe instead of exiting when it's absent. The host process stays alive → Chrome's native port stays connected → the service worker stays alive → **no more flapping**.
- Simple request/response relay: read `getWindows` from the pipe → Chrome → read the reply from stdin → back to the pipe. When the app disposes its per-capture server, the host loops back and waits for the next one. It exits only when Chrome closes the port (stdin EOF).

No app changes, no manifest/registry changes. Also added a regression test for the hang and updated `README.md` (Chrome in the intro feature list) and `docs/spikes/browser.md` (patient-host behavior). **All 109 tests pass.**

## To see it work live

The two stale host processes (PIDs 32104, 33000) from the old build are still running. Just:
1. Go to `chrome://extensions` → reload the **Sessions** extension (this kills the old hosts; the new `BrowserHost.dll` loads on the next connect).
2. Open a Chrome window with a couple of tabs, then Save a session in the app — the Chrome window should capture its tabs now, and the console spam should stop.

If it still misreports, the console there will tell us which leg (host vs. extension) — ping me.

## Commit message (yours to make)

```
fix: keep the browser host alive so Chrome capture works

The host connected to the app's pipe once at launch and exited when the
app wasn't mid-capture, so it flapped (Chrome relaunching it every second)
and a save only captured Chrome if a host launch happened to land in the
~3s pipe window. Make the host wait for the pipe instead of exiting: it
blocks on Connect until the app opens its server, relays one request/reply,
then loops back for the next capture, staying alive (and keeping the service
worker's port up) in between. Exit only when Chrome closes the port.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

This is a second, separable change from the hang fix — want me to keep them as two commits (hang fix + this), or is one combined commit fine for your workflow?

This new error is the title-match step: with two or more Chrome windows, matching an OS window to its tabs purely by active-tab title is ambiguous (your two windows are both on a NeetCode/YouTube page, exactly the case the hint warns about). The reliable discriminator is **window position**, which we already capture on the OS side but don't use.

Let me look at the pieces involved.

The handshake works now; this is the title-match step failing. The most likely cause is title drift between the OS window title and the tab title — browsers prepend an unread/notification count like `(1) ` to the tab title (very common on YouTube), and the two are sampled a moment apart, so the exact string compare misses and, with a second background Chrome window present, it reports ambiguity.

The safe, app-side fix is to normalize both titles before comparing (strip a leading `(n) ` count, trim). No extension change or reload needed. Let me make it.

Notably, that flaky failure was real-world proof the patient-host fix works end to end: a live `BrowserHost` on your machine connected to the test's pipe, relayed to Chrome, and the extension returned **actual window data**. The host↔extension↔Chrome round-trip is healthy now.

## This change: robust title matching

The match from an OS window to its Chrome-reported tabs was an exact string compare. Browsers prepend an unread/notification count like `(1) ` to the tab title (YouTube does this constantly), and the OS title vs. the tab title are sampled a moment apart — so the window failed to match itself, and with a second Chrome window open, the capture was reported as ambiguous. That's your `NeetCode - YouTube` failure.

- `BrowserAdapter.NormalizeTitle` now strips a leading `(n) ` count and trims before comparing, both sides. Fixes drift in either direction.
- Added two tests covering count-on-tab and count-on-window-title.
- Also made `BrowserTabsClient.Query` take an optional pipe name (a test seam) so the pipe tests don't collide with a real host on the production pipe name — that's what caused the flake.

This is **app-side only** — no extension or host change. Just rebuild and relaunch the Sessions app:

```
dotnet run --project src/Sessions.App
```

One honest caveat: if you genuinely have **two Chrome windows open on the same page**, that's still reported as ambiguous by design — title alone can't tell them apart. If you hit that for real, the fix is position-based disambiguation (match the captured window's screen position to Chrome's reported bounds), which needs an extension change and careful DPI handling on a high-DPI laptop like yours. Say the word and I'll do it.

## Commit message (yours to make)

```
fix: match Chrome windows through notification-count title drift

The OS window title and the extension's tab title are sampled a moment
apart, and browsers prepend an unread count like "(1) " to the tab title
(YouTube especially), so an exact compare failed to match a window to its
own tabs and, with another Chrome window open, reported the capture as
ambiguous. Normalize both titles (drop a leading "(n) " count, trim) before
comparing. Also give Query an injectable pipe name so the pipe tests don't
bind the production name a live host may hold.

No no — multiple tabs in **one window** is exactly the normal case and fully works. That's the whole point of the feature.

Here's the distinction:

- **One Chrome window with many tabs** → captured as a single entry holding *all* its tab URLs, and Load reopens them together in one window (`chrome.exe --new-window url1 url2 url3 …`). Totally supported. The `BrowserEntry.Urls` list is the full tab list for that window.
- **Multiple separate Chrome windows** → each window becomes its own entry. This is where matching matters: the app has to figure out *which* OS window is *which* reported window, and it does that by the active tab's title.

The ambiguity caveat only bites in one narrow case: you have **two or more separate windows** whose *active* tabs happen to show the **same title** at the moment of capture — then the app can't tell those windows apart.
